title: Desire, gently
hookLine: for now, don't desire what isn't up to you; only choose and refuse lightly (Enchiridion 2)

cards: Every want comes with a promise tucked inside it. Want the job, and the want quietly promises: you'll get it. Dread the diagnosis, and the dread promises: you'll escape it.

The promise is easy to miss until it breaks, and then the disappointment can seem like something done to us. Section two of the handbook takes those promises seriously. It doesn't tell a beginner to stop wanting forever.
It says something gentler, and odder, with two small words that matter a lot: for now.

teach.b: Desire, Epictetus says, promises that you'll get what you desire; aversion promises that you won't fall into what you avoid. Miss what you desire and you feel unlucky. Fall into what you avoid and you feel wretched.
So move aversion home. If you only push away things in your own power, like your own cruelty or cowardice, you'll never fall into them against your will.

teach.h: AVOID ONLY WHAT IS YOURS TO AVOID.
teach.b: Try to avoid sickness, death or poverty, and you've signed up for misery, because those aren't yours to avoid. So he says: take aversion off everything outside your power, and set it on the things inside it.
For the present, he says, set desire aside completely.
Desire what isn't up to you and you're bound to be disappointed, and the good things that are up to you, a steady character, sound judgment, aren't yet within a beginner's reach.
This is advice for someone starting out, not a rule for a whole life.
Meanwhile, use only choosing and refusing, moving toward a thing or away from it, and do even that lightly, without straining, with a reservation. The Stoics meant a quiet clause attached to a plan.
Seneca gives one: I'll sail, unless something gets in the way.

Neighbors say something close. Muslims say in sha Allah, if God wills, and the letter of James in the New Testament says to speak of plans with: if the Lord will. Epictetus' version is simply: lightly, and for now.

how: Some Stoic practitioners add a quiet reservation to their plans, such as 'if nothing prevents me', so they can act fully while holding the outcome lightly.

o: a passing mood that has nothing to do with choice
any feeling at all, which Stoics try to erase
a want that promises you'll get what you reach for

s: Epictetus tells everyone to give up desire for the rest of their life
he says 'for the present': it's advice for someone just starting out.
he says to avoid only things that are in your own power
avoid sickness or death and you're bound to fall into what you avoid.
the Stoics attached a quiet reservation to their plans
something like: I'll go, if nothing prevents me.

games.q: you're new to the handbook and you badly want a promotion. what does section two suggest, for now?
o: want it with everything you've got.
set the desire down and choose your steps lightly.
games.why: for a beginner, Epictetus says: set desire aside for now, and choose and refuse lightly, with a reservation.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you want that isn't fully up to you, a reply, a result, a yes from someone, and feel where the want pulls in your body.
Without pushing it away, add the quiet clause inside: I'd like this, if nothing prevents it. You're still allowed to want it; you're just holding it in an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Desire. In the handbook, a want that promises to get. For a beginner, Epictetus says: set it down for now, and choose lightly instead. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, Enchiridion 2: desire, a reaching out toward something.

carryVoice: Your line: gently, for now. A plan can carry a quiet unless and still be a real plan. That's day three hundred thirty-four.
